title: Wendell and the Language
premise: Lior Ravensworth, once a celebrated composition prodigy, returns to the Aldermoor Conservatory as a night janitor after a decade of silence following his mother's death and his own disappearance from the music world. When he hears an unfinished lullaby she wrote—never recorded, never published—playing on a late-night radio program, he realizes someone has her notebooks, and that the man in the old photographs, his mother's secret collaborator and possible betrayer, is still alive and teaching nearby. As Lior infiltrates the conservatory's archives to recover her work, he must choose between exposing the truth of what was stolen from her and protecting the loyal friend who has kept her memory alive at terrible personal cost. He ends by performing her finished piece publicly under both their names, forgiving the stranger in the photographs—and finally himself.
about_author: Elodie Fairweather is the pen name of a former conservatory archivist who spent years cataloguing unpublished manuscripts by forgotten women composers. She writes literary fiction about music, memory, and the quiet violence of institutions.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Ten years after vanishing from the concert stage, Lior mops the Aldermoor Conservatory's practice halls at night, cataloguing in a notebook everything students leave unsaid in their playing. The beat is numb routine masking grief—he passes his mother's old classroom without stopping.

chapters.title: A Song on the Frequency
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In his basement flat, a late-night radio program plays a fragment of 'Vespers for a Small Room'—a lullaby his mother composed and never recorded, which he burned with her papers. Shaken, he realizes someone else possesses her notebooks. The beat: the past breaking through sealed doors.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photographs
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Sorting a box of his mother's belongings, he studies the only photograph of her collaborator, Tomas Veyra—a young man laughing beside her at the conservatory, decades ago. His mother never spoke his name aloud. The beat: suspicion kindling into obsession.

chapters.title: Night Shift, Third Floor
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Working the archive wing after hours, Lior discovers Veyra is now composer-in-residence at Aldermoor himself, one floor above where Lior cleans. They nearly meet in a stairwell; Veyra doesn't recognize him. The beat: vertigo of proximity to the enemy.

chapters.title: What the Students Leave Behind
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A gifted but struggling student, Maren Okafor, begins leaving her failed sketches in the practice room trash; Lior secretly reads them and recognizes his younger self. He starts leaving anonymous corrections. The beat: reluctant tenderness, the first crack in his invisibility.

chapters.title: The Archive's Locked Drawer
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Using a janitor's master key, Lior finds the restricted manuscript collection and locates a folder labeled 'R.' Inside: pages of his mother's handwriting he's never seen. But the folder is checked out—to T. Veyra. The beat: cold confirmation that the theft is ongoing.

chapters.title: Lessons in Borrowed Light
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren notices the janitor who seems to understand her music better than her professors, and begins seeking him out between shifts. She confides her fear that talent means losing yourself. The beat: an unlikely apprenticeship forming across class lines.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior tracks down the radio host, who admits the recording came from a private donor to the station—an anonymous bequest tied to the Veyra Foundation. The song is being released, movement by movement, as if someone is curating his mother posthumously. The beat: dread that exposure may serve someone else's redemption.

chapters.title: The Loyalty of Small Betrayals
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Flashback chapter: young Lior, eighteen, discovering his mother's notebooks missing days before her death, and choosing not to confront Veyra because the man had paid for her hospice care. The beat: the original sin—survival purchased with silence.

chapters.title: Concerto for One Listener
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior attends Veyra's faculty recital incognito and hears him perform 'Vespers' complete, credited as 'traditional, arr. Veyra.' Lior's hands shake so badly he leaves at intermission. The beat: rage crystallizing into resolve.

chapters.title: Maren Asks the Wrong Question
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren asks the janitor why he quit music, having deduced he trained somewhere serious. Lior deflects cruelly, wounding her. Alone, she plays 'Vespers' from memory—she heard it on the radio too—and something in Lior breaks open. The beat: connection nearly severed, then deepened by accident.

chapters.title: The Foundation's Paper Trail
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. With help from a sympathetic records clerk, Lior traces the Veyra Foundation's acquisitions: dozens of unpublished works by dead or disappeared composers, all 'arranged' by Veyra, all generating royalties. His mother is one name among many. The beat: private grief becoming systemic indictment.

chapters.title: An Invitation He Should Refuse
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Veyra, having glimpsed Lior's face in the stairwell light, invites the 'janitor with the careful ears' to critique his new arrangement. Lior accepts, planning reconnaissance, and finds himself genuinely moved by Veyra's musicianship. The beat: the enemy becoming human—the novel's moral hinge.

chapters.title: The Hospice Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior obtains the old billing records and learns the truth: Veyra sold his own compositions to fund her care, then took her notebooks as collateral and could never give them back without confessing the theft that funded her survival. The beat: justice and mercy colliding; no clean villain.

chapters.title: What Maren Deserves to Know
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren discovers Lior's identity from an old competition poster and confronts him: he abandoned music while lecturing her about courage. Her anger forces him to speak his mother's name aloud for the first time in ten years. The beat: shame transmuted into testimony.

chapters.title: Two Men, One Room
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior confronts Veyra directly, laying out the ledgers, the radio broadcasts, the archive withdrawals. Veyra neither denies nor apologizes; he plays the final unfinished movement and says, 'Finish it, then. You're the only one who can.' The beat: climax of confrontation—truth offered as inheritance, not restitution.

chapters.title: The Weight of the Pen
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Alone with the complete notebooks, Lior spends three nights attempting the final movement and cannot—until he stops trying to restore her voice and lets his own answer hers. The duet completes itself. The beat: forgiveness of the stranger in the photographs, who was always also himself.

chapters.title: Terms Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior declines to pursue legal action; instead he negotiates privately: the foundation funds publication of all recovered composers under their true names, Veyra retires from teaching, and no one goes to prison. Maren calls it cowardice; Lior calls it the only justice that doesn't burn the music too. The beat: costly, imperfect resolution.

chapters.title: Program Notes
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Preparing the premiere, Lior writes honest program notes naming his mother, Veyra's debts, and his own decade of silence. The conservatory threatens to cancel; Maren organizes the students. The beat: the institution versus the truth, with the young taking sides.

chapters.title: Vespers, Complete
chapters.summary: Alternating Lior and Maren POVs. In a small hall, Lior performs 'Vespers for a Small Room' publicly for the first time—mother's movements, then his completion—with Veyra watching from the last row. Maren plays the second piano part. The beat: catharsis; the inventory of unsaid things finally spoken in sound.

chapters.title: After the Applause
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Backstage, Lior and Veyra share a brief, unhealed peace—two men who survived each other. Veyra returns the original photograph. Lior does not forgive him fully, and knows he never will, and that this is enough. The beat: mature acceptance over tidy absolution.

chapters.title: The Morning Shift
chapters.summary: Lior's POV, epilogue. Months later, Lior still cleans the conservatory—but now teaches one composition seminar and keeps his mother's completed score on the archive shelf under her full name. A new student leaves a sketch in the trash; he picks it up. The beat: quiet continuation; survival, at last, worth its price.
